source.title: Do Unlearning Methods Remove Information from Language Model Weights?

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether unlearning removes information by fine-tuning on independent facts and measuring recovery. It finds strong recovery for pretrained information, but weaker recovery for some methods on fine-tuned information.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses prompting attacks, activation directions, quantization, and other studies’ jailbreak results, but does not test those itself. Figure-only accuracy results are recorded without estimating plotted values. Cited results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study builds a retraining-on-T attack (T and V are disjoint, independent facts from the same unlearned set) and measures recovery on V after GD, RMU and RIA unlearning on Llama 3 8B. It also tests WMDP's released RMU zephyr model and a RepNoise model. Recovery exceeds 88% for pretrained information, which bears directly on A and B. It also tests one fine-tuning-robust method (F).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that the tested methods remove only a small fraction of information learned in pretraining, so it is hidden, not removed. They recommend RTT-style recovery attacks for evaluating unlearning. They also conclude that evaluations on fine-tuned information (Random Birthdays) overestimate robustness, so testing should use pretrained information.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces an adversarial retraining-on-T evaluation rather than reproducing an original method's evaluation. It applies Gradient Difference, RMU, and Random Incorrect Answer as the tested unlearning methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery differs by whether information was learned during pretraining or an additional fine-tuning phase, and by unlearning method on Random Birthdays. The study also varies dataset format, retain-accuracy drop, RTT loss, learning rate, and training epochs.
record.problems: RTT requires fine-tuning and hyperparameter search and does not guarantee that information is absent from the weights. The authors say the evaluation depends on low-leakage fact sets, may miss hiding distributed across separate parts of a model, and does not cover capability unlearning. The study reports only one fine-tuned-information dataset. Many plotted results do not have individual numeric values stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results were left out. Cited jailbreak, prompting, quantization, and activation-edit results were excluded because they are not results of this study.

untested.parts: Prompt-based attacks (rephrasing, jailbreaks); general-ability checks beyond the ≤5% retain-accuracy drop setting.
Small or few-shot relearning sets; unrelated or loosely related relearning data. Only a medium-scale set (628 facts from the forget distribution) is used.
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis.
No prompting, jailbreak, language or in-context attacks.
Only RepNoise is tested; TAR and other robust methods are only cited.

missing.what: Recovery after RTT at retain-accuracy drops of 10%, 30% and 100%, and the RMU retain-coefficient sweep. RTT still recovers accuracy even with no retain loss, or when retain accuracy falls to 25%.
Effect of unlearning-data format (WMDP forget corpora, GPT-4o plain text, MCQ variants) on GD/RMU forget accuracy and RTT recovery
With an earlier Random Birthdays version containing duplicate names, RTT did recover GD/RIA-unlearned information

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source; r25 uses an original source's released model. r24 and r26 duplicate one result. T (628 facts) is medium-scale, so 'small relearning set' in B is only loosely met. The fine-tuned-information null result relies on one dataset.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests whether RTT recovers targeted performance after unlearning. It does not test rephrasing, jailbreaks, or other attacks that do not use facts from the forget distribution.

The attack uses four of five fact splits (628 datapoints), not a few examples; it is not an attack using unrelated or loosely related examples. It does test a subset of facts from the same distribution.
No activation-direction ablation or internal edit is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context-information attack is tested.
The paper tests RTT against RepNoise, a method targeting fine-tuning robustness. It does not test a method shown to resist all the listed attack types.

tranche.reason: Its own RTT results show unlearned pretrained knowledge is mostly hidden rather than removed. This bears against A and restates how unlearning should be evaluated.

source_check.notes: Per-cell accuracies are figure-only. The text states recovery rates >88% for all pretrained-information cells at ≤5% retain drop. Recovery rate is the ratio of unlearned+RTT to original+RTT accuracy, so it is not directly comparable with the 31.2% no-knowledge accuracy control (App E). The Random Birthdays results depend on the de-duplicated dataset (App L). The RepNoise model's size and dataset are not named.

statements.correction: 2410.08827 Appendix C: RTT on the RepNoise model supplied by its authors. Wide learning-rate and epoch search. Trains on low-leakage subsets (T) of the dataset RepNoise was applied to and scores the held-out subset (V), not WMDP-Bio. Recovers accuracy as well as fine-tuning the original model (figure only, Fig. 6).
statements.problem: The 2410.08827 clause gets the method wrong: it says 'retraining on held-out facts', but RTT trains on split T and scores the held-out split V. The umbrella condition 'fine-tuning attacks on WMDP-Bio' also does not fit this study's RepNoise test.
